title: Vimalakirti is ill
hookLine: a wealthy layman of Vaishali lies sick, and the Buddha wants someone to visit him

lines: A RICH MAN SICK IN VAISHALI.
cards: In the city of Vaishali, a rich man is in bed, sick. Word gets around, and the visitors start coming: princes and ministers, merchants, townspeople, priests and householders.
He's glad to see every one of them, and from his sickbed, propped on the pillows, he teaches them. His name is Vimalakirti.

The sutra named for him, one of the books Kumarajiva put into Chinese, says something odd right away. His illness is a skillful means. He is sick on purpose, for the sake of the people who come to see him.

teach.b: First, who he is. Vimalakirti isn't a monk. He's a householder, with a wife and children, servants, money, and a place in the life of his city.
The sutra shows him moving through all of it: the markets, the law courts, the schools, even the gambling halls and the drinking houses.

He keeps a householder's clothes and a householder's life, and everywhere he goes, the sutra says, he's there to bring people toward the teaching: a layman whose wisdom matches the great bodhisattvas.
Now the sickbed. When the visitors come, he doesn't talk about his fever. He talks about the body.
It's like a ball of foam that can't be squeezed, he tells them. Like a bubble that doesn't last. Like a mirage, a dream, a reflection, like the trunk of a plantain tree, with no hard core inside.
A list meant to unsettle. But listen to where he takes it. He doesn't tell them to despise the body.
He tells them to turn toward a different kind of body, the body of a Buddha, made of generosity, patience, wisdom and kindness.
The sick body becomes a door. Then the scene turns.
Lying there, Vimalakirti thinks: I'm sick. Won't the Buddha send someone to ask after me? And the Buddha, knowing his thought, turns to his disciples and asks who will go.

how: The Vimalakirti Sutra is read across Mahayana traditions, and in East Asia Vimalakirti became a model of the lay practitioner: someone with a household and a job whose practice is carried out in ordinary life.

o: a king who gave his whole city to the Buddha
a wealthy layman who teaches from his sickbed
a monk who left his family to live in the forest

p: a householder of Vaishali, not a monk
a skillful means, for his visitors
asks who will go and visit him

s: Vimalakirti is a monk who has left home
he's a householder, with a family, wealth and a place in his city.
he teaches his visitors from his sickbed
princes, merchants and townspeople come, and he teaches them about the body.
he tells his visitors to despise the body
he points them past the fragile body toward the body of a Buddha, made of good qualities.

games.q: you're Vimalakirti, sick in bed, and the whole city is coming to visit. what do you talk about?
o: your symptoms and how you're feeling.
the body: fragile as foam, and a door to something else.
nothing; you ask them to let you rest.
games.why: he teaches that the body is like foam, a bubble, a mirage, and turns them toward the body of a Buddha.

practice: Feel your own body as it is today, the aches and the ease. Then bring to mind someone who is sick, tired or stuck at home, and in your imagination sit down beside them, the way the visitors sat beside Vimalakirti.
You don't need to fix anything or say anything wise; just be the one who came.

wordCard.voice: Vimalakirti. The wealthy layman of Vaishali who lies sick for the sake of his visitors, and teaches them from his bed. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the layman of Vaishali at the center of this sutra.

carryVoice: Your line: the sick layman. Even a sickbed can be a place to teach. That's today, done.
